{{nihongo|'''Amenotoyotarashikarahimenomikoto Shrine'''|天豊足柄姫命神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Iwami Province]].

'''Amen o-Toyotarashikarahimenomikoto Shrine''' (あめのとよたらしからひめのみことじんじゃ) is a Shinto shrine located in {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|Q132751|qid=Q132751}}, {{ill|Hamada, Shimane|Q432055|qid=Q432055}}. It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}}, and its former shrine rank was {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Prefectural shrine}}.

=== Enshrined deities ===
The main enshrined deity is {{ill|Ameno-Toyotarashikarahimenomikoto|Q24863814|qid=Q24863814}} (あめのとよたらしからひめのみこと), with {{ill|Toyouke-hime|Q2983724|qid=Q2983724|lt=Toyoukehimenomikoto}} enshrined together. The subsidiary shrine within the precincts, Kameyama Shrine, enshrines successive lords of the Hamada Domain.
Although the deeds of the main deity are not clearly known, she is revered as a goddess who taught the ways of clothing and food.
The former *History of Shimane Prefecture* argues regarding Ameno-Toyotarashikarahimenomikoto: “The stone deity is merely a temporary vessel of a single generation; the true enshrined deity is Ameno-Toyotarashikarahimenomikoto.”

=== History ===
The circumstances of the shrine’s founding are unknown. It is presumed to have flourished as a Shikinaisha, but from the medieval period onward it declined amid continued warfare, remaining in ruin for several hundred years. In the Meiji period, following the abolition of the domains and establishment of prefectures, a new shrine building was erected. In Meiji 6 (1873) it became a prefectural shrine, and in July of Meiji 8 (1875) it became a village shrine.

In Bunmei 18 (1486), the shrine buildings were reconstructed.
In Genna 6 (1620), Furuta Shigeharu entered Hamada from Matsusaka in Ise Province, constructed Hamada Castle, and enshrined the deity within the castle grounds.
In Meiji 7 (1874), both the main hall and the worship hall were constructed.

{{Quotation|
The stone deity is a god enshrining Ameno-Toyotarashikarahimenomikoto of Iwami. According to its tradition, the notion that the deity turned into stone has no basis and cannot be believed. It is surmised that the deity opened up Iwami Province and bestowed merit upon the people, who, admiring and revering this virtue, built a shrine hall and enshrined the deity. Considering that it is listed as a Shikinaisha, one can know how large the shrine hall was at that time and how solemn and prosperous the worship was. From the medieval period onward, calamities and unrest continued, worship could not be carried out, and it fell into ruin for several hundred years. In the Meiji era, domains were abolished and prefectures established, and Nobuhiro came to govern this region. He reported to the Imperial Court his reverence for the kami, and as this place had an association with the stone deity, restoration thereafter began. Here, a new shrine hall was built and worship resumed; it was deliberated to make it a prefectural shrine and to encourage the prefectural people to venerate it perpetually.
This was inscribed on stone in order to record this matter.
January, Meiji 7
| Governor of Hamada Prefecture, Senior Sixth Rank, Sato Nobuhiro, composed | Explanation of the monument inscription}}
